Surah al-Dukhan (The Smoke) is Meccan, except for His saying ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little[, but you will return]﴾, and its verses number fifty-nine.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book.﴾ The discussion regarding this is like that which preceded in the previous surah.

Surah al-Dukhan (The Smoke) is Meccan, except for His saying ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little[, but you will return]﴾, and its verses number fifty-nine.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book.﴾ The discussion regarding this is like that which preceded in the previous surah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾. That is: the Clear Book (al-kitab al-mubin), which is the Qur'an.

﴿in a blessed night﴾. It is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). It was also said: it is the Night of Acquittal (Laylat al-Bara'a), in which its revelation began, or in which it was sent down all at once from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) to the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya), and Jibril, peace be upon him, dictated it to the scribes (al-safara), and then he used to bring it down to the Prophet (ﷺ) in installments over twenty-three years, as has been mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Fatiha. Describing it as blessed is because the descent of the Qur'an entails all the religious and worldly benefits together, or because in it there is the descent of the angels, mercy, the answering of supplication, the distribution of blessings, the decision of judgments, the excellence of worship, and the granting of the complete intercession to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: the water of Zamzam increases on this night by a clearly visible increase.

﴿Indeed, We have always been warners﴾. This is a resumptive clause explaining the reason for the decree of the sending down, as if it were said: We sent it down because it is part of Our way to warn and to caution against punishment. It was also said: it is the answer to the oath, and His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ ...etc. is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). It was also said: it is a second answer, without a conjunction.

Here is the translation:

﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), like what precedes it, for its being the time when the wise matters are distinguished, whether those that are firmly established or those that are ambiguous, in accordance with the wisdom that agrees with them, necessarily calls for the Qur'an, which is among its greatest matters, to be sent down in it. It has been said: it is another attribute of "a night" (laylah), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD). This indicates that it is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr). The meaning of "yufraqu" (is made distinct) is that it is recorded and separated: every wise matter concerning the provisions and lifespans of the servants, and all their affairs, from this night until the next year. It has been said: the copying of that from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) begins on the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'ah), and the completion occurs on the Night of Decree, so the copy of provisions is handed over to Mika'il, the copy of wars to Jibril, likewise earthquakes, landslides and thunderbolts, and the copy of deeds to Isma'il, the lord of the lowest heaven, who is a mighty angel, and the copy of calamities to the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. It is also read "yufarraqu" with doubled letter, and it is read "yafruqu" in the active form, meaning: God Most High makes every wise matter distinct (p-59), and it is read "nafruqu" with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah).

ۣ﴿Amran min ʿindina﴾ is put in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: "I mean by this matter a matter issuing from Us, in accordance with the requirement of Our wisdom." It explains the greatness of the relational aspect after explaining its intrinsic greatness. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "kullu amrin" (every matter), since it is specified by the description, or of the pronoun in "hakim" (wise). It has also been permitted that it denote the opposite of prohibition (nahy), and be taken as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muakkid), in order to distinguish it, since "amr" (command) and "furqan" (criterion) are identical in meaning; or that it be governed by its implied verb, since the distinction is made by it; or that it be a circumstantial qualifier of one of the two pronouns in "anzalnahu," meaning: "commanding" or "commanded."

﴿Inna kunna mursilin﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "Inna kunna mundhirin" (indeed We were warners). It has been said that it is a third answer (jawab thalith). It has also been said that it is a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnaf).

Translation of the passage:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾ is an end (ghayah) for the sending down (al-irsal), delayed relative to it, on the understanding that by it is meant the mercy that reaches the servants, a motive (ba'ith) preceding it. Or it is meant as its origin (mabda'uha), i.e., "We sent down the Qur'an because it is Our custom to send messengers with scriptures to the servants in order to pour out Our mercy upon them, or because Our previous mercy necessitates sending them." The placing of "your Lord" (al-Rabb) in the position of a pronoun is to indicate that this is among the rulings and requirements of lordship (rububiyyah), and its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, is for his honour. Or it is a causal clause for "is made distinct" (yufraq), or for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a command﴾ (amran). Or ﴿mercy﴾ is an object of the sending (irsal), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever He withholds, none can send it forth after Him﴾ (fa-la mursila lahu), meaning: in it every matter is made distinct, or the commands issue from Us, because it is Our custom to send Our mercy. There is no doubt that each of the distribution of provisions and other things, and the commands issuing from Him, exalted is He, is of the category of mercy, for the purpose of imposing worship is to expose the servants to benefits. It was also read as "rahmatun" in the nominative, meaning: that is a mercy. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is a confirmation of His lordship, exalted is He, and that it is not due except to one who has these attributes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 7:

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is either a substitution (badal) for [Your Lord], or an explanatory apposition (bayan), or a qualifier (na't). It is also read in the nominative (bi-al-raf'), on the basis that it is another predicate (khabar akhar), or as a new sentence (istinaf) with an implied subject (mubtada') elided.

﴿If you are people of certainty (muqinin)﴾ means: if you are among the people of certainty (ahl al-iqan) in knowledge, or, if you are certain (muqinin) in your acknowledgment that He, exalted is He, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, when you are asked, "Who created them?" and you say, "God," then you know that the matter is as we have said. Or it means: if you are seekers of certainty (muridin al-yaqin), then know that.

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʾnafa*, an independent sentence that begins a new statement) that confirms what precedes it. It has also been said that it is the predicate (*khabar*) of His saying ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ etc., and that what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtirāḍ*).

﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a resumptive clause, as the one before it is. The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your earliest forefathers﴾, which is either by supposing an implied subject (*mubtadaʾ*, the topic of a nominal sentence) or is an apposition (*badal*) to "Lord of the heavens" according to the recitation with the *raf*ʿ (nominative), or an explicative apposition (*bayān*) or a qualifier (*naʿt*, adjective) to it. It has also been said that it is the subject (*fāʿil*) of "causes death", and that in "gives life" there is a pronoun (*ḍamīr*) referring back to "Lord of the heavens". It has been recited with the *jarr* (genitive), as an apposition to "Lord of the heavens" according to the recitation with the *jarr*.

﴿Rather, they are in doubt﴾ about the matters of Him, exalted is He, that were mentioned; they are not certain in their affirmation.

﴿playing﴾: they do not say what they say in earnest or with conviction, but mixed with mockery and play.(p-60)

The fa' in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So watch﴾ is for the sequencing of the watching or of the command to it upon what precedes it, for their being in doubt is something that necessarily requires that. That is, wait for them.

﴿The day when the sky will bring a manifest smoke﴾ That is, a day of severity and famine, for the hungry person sees between himself and the sky something like the appearance of smoke, either because of the weakness of his sight, or because in a year of drought the air becomes dark due to scarce rain and abundant dust, or because the Arabs call an overwhelming evil "smoke." This is because when Quraysh disobeyed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he invoked against them, saying: ﴿O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make it upon them as years of Joseph.﴾ So a year of drought seized them, until they ate carrion, bones, and al-'ilhiz (a blood-and-hair mixture). A man would see smoke between the sky and the earth, and he would speak to a man whose words he heard but could not see because of the smoke. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 11:

﴿Covering over the people.﴾ That is: it envelops them.

﴿This is a painful punishment.﴾ That is: saying this. Then Abu Sufyan and a group with him came to him, upon whom be prayers and peace, and they appealed to him by Allah the Exalted and by the ties of kinship, and promised him that if he prayed for them and removed it from them, they would believe. And that is the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 12:

﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers.﴾ This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, and Mujahid and Muqatil adopted it, and it is the preference of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It has also been said: it is a smoke that comes from the sky before the Day of Resurrection, and it enters the ears of the disbelievers until the head of each one becomes like a roasted head, and the believer is afflicted by it in the manner of a cold in the head, and the whole earth becomes like a house that has been set alight in which there is no gap. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The first of the signs is the smoke, and the descent of 'Isa son of Maryam, and a fire that comes out from the depths of 'Adan Abyan, driving the people to the place of gathering." Hudhayfah said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the smoke?" So he recited the verse and said: "It fills what is between the east and the west, and remains for forty days and nights. As for the believer, it afflicts him like a cold in the head, and as for the disbeliever, he is like a drunkard, coming out from his nostrils, his ears and his posterior." The first view is the one that the course of the noble arrangement of the verses clearly requires.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 13:

Indeed, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How will they have the reminder?﴾ ...etc., is a rejection of their statement and their request for the removal (of the punishment), and a denial of them regarding their promise of faith, which indicates remembrance and admonition by what the calamity has befallen them. That is: how can they remember, or from where can they remember with that, and fulfil what they promised Him of faith at the removal of the punishment from them?

﴿And there had already come to them a clear Messenger﴾. That is: while the situation is that they witnessed, of the motives for remembrance and the requirements of admonition, what is greater than it in necessitating them, in that there had come to them a Messenger of great standing, who made clear to them the paths of truth by displaying manifest signs and compelling miracles, before which the deaf mountains would prostrate.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 14:

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾ from that Messenger, and he was the very same one. (They did so) as soon as they witnessed from him what they had witnessed of the great signs that call for turning towards him, and they were not content with merely turning away.

﴿And they said﴾ concerning him:

﴿A taught, possessed man﴾ That is: at one time they said, "He is taught by a non-Arab (a'jami) slave belonging to some of the Thaqif," and at another time, "He is possessed (majnun)," or some of them would say one thing and others another. So how could one expect from a people with these characteristics that they would be affected by admonition and reminder? Their likeness is only that of the dog: when it is hungry it pants, and when it is satisfied it becomes insolent (taghā).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 15:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾ is a response from Him, Exalted is He, to their saying: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾, by way of iltifat (the shift in grammatical person) for greater reproach and threat, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). That is: Indeed, We will remove the known punishment from you a little (kashfan qalilan), or for a little time, [but] indeed you will return, immediately after that, to what you were upon of obstinacy and persistence in disbelief, and you will forget this state. The form of the active participle (sighah al-fa'il) in both verbs is to indicate that both will certainly occur. And both have indeed happened, since God, Exalted is He, removed the punishment through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ), then they soon returned to what they had been upon of obstinacy and stubbornness. As for the one who interpreted the smoke (al-dukhan) as being among the minor signs (al-ashrat) of the Hour, he said: When the smoke comes, the punished among the disbelievers and hypocrites will writhe because of it, and they will cry out for help and say: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾. Then God, Exalted is He, will remove it from them after forty [days], and as soon as He removes it from them, they will revert and will not delay.

On the Day We seize with the greatest seizing (﴿يَوْمَ نَبْطِشُ البَطْشَةَ الكُبْرى﴾). This is the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: the Day of Badr. It is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) governed by what is indicated by His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Indeed We will take vengeance﴾ (﴿إنّا مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾), not by "will take vengeance" itself, because "indeed" (inna) prevents that. That is, on that day We will take vengeance; indeed We will take vengeance. It is also said that it is a substitute (badal) for "the Day when there comes..." etc.

It is read "nubtishu" (نُبْطِشُ), meaning: We cause the angels to seize them with the greatest seizing, which is taking hold forcefully and with dominance; or We make the greatest seizing seize them. It is also read "nabtushu" (نَبْطُشُ) with a damma on the ṭā', and this is a dialect (lughah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 17:

﴿And We certainly tested before them the people of Pharaoh﴾. That is: We tested them by sending Musa, peace be upon him, or We placed them in trial by granting them respite and widening their provision. It is also read with the doubled consonant (fattana, shaddah), for emphasis or because of the multitude of the people.

﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾ noble in the sight of Allah the Exalted, or in the sight of the believers, and noble in himself, because Allah the Exalted never sent a prophet except from among the chiefs and nobles of his people.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 44, verse 18:

﴿Ann addu ilayya ʿibāda Allāh﴾ means: "that you should deliver to me the servants of God," i.e., either by delivering the Children of Israel to me and sending them with me, or by delivering to me, O servants of God, their due of faith and acceptance of the call. It has been said that "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (mufassira), since the coming of a messenger can only be with a message and a call. It has also been said that it is a lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqīla), meaning: he came to them saying that the matter is: deliver to me... etc.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Innī lakum rasūlun amīn﴾ ("Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger") is a justification for the command, or for the obligation of what is commanded, meaning: a messenger who is not suspect (ghayr ẓanīn), whom God, exalted is He, has entrusted with His revelation and has confirmed through overpowering miracles.

"And do not exalt yourselves against Allah"; that is, do not be arrogant toward Him, the Exalted, by treating His revelation and His Messenger with contempt. The "an" (that) here is like the one that preceded. His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, I am coming to you" means: from His side, the Exalted. (p-62) "with a clear authority" is the reason for the prohibition; that is, I come to you with a manifest proof for which there is no way to deny. "Ataakum" may be read in the form of the active participle or the imperfect. In placing the verb "I come" with the trustworthy one and the authority with the exalted, there is a degree of eloquence that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 20:

﴿And indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾. That is: I have taken refuge in Him and placed my trust in Him.

﴿Lest you stone me﴾. Meaning: lest you stone me, that is, harm me by beating or reviling me, or kill me. It was said: when he said, "And do not exalt yourselves against Allah," they threatened him with killing.

Note: the reading with idgham (assimilation) of the dhal into the ta' was also transmitted.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone.﴾

That is: even if you stubbornly oppose the demands of reason and do not believe me, then leave me be, neither for me nor against me, and do not confront me with evil or harm. For that would not be the reward of one who calls you to that in which your welfare lies. Interpreting it to mean "then sever the bonds of connection with me, so that there is no friendship between me and you and those who do not believe" is rejected by the context (yaba'uhu al-maqam).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 22:

﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾ after they persisted in denying him, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed these are﴾, meaning: that these are.

﴿a criminal people﴾. This is an allusion (ta'rid) to supplicating against them by mentioning what they deserved, and for this reason it is called a supplication. It is also read with a kasra on the initial letter (inna), on the assumption of an implied verb of saying (al-qawl). It was said: his supplication was, "O Allah, hasten for them what they deserve for their crimes." It was also said: it was his saying, ﴿"Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people."﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 23:

﴿So set out with My servants by night﴾ with the verb of saying being understood (idmar al-qawl), either after the fa' (so the meaning is: "Then his Lord said: Set out with My servants"), or before it, as if it were said: "If the matter is as you say, then set out with My servants," that is, with the Children of Israel, for God the Exalted has arranged that you should go ahead. It is also read with a connecting hamza (wasl al-hamza) from "sara" (to travel by night).

﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾, that is: Pharaoh and his hosts will follow you after they have come to know of your departure.

**Qur'anic quotation:** ﴿And leave the sea ajar﴾ — open, with a wide gap, or still in its state after you have crossed it; and do not strike it with your staff so that it closes, nor change it from its condition so that the Copts may enter it.

﴿Indeed they are an army to be drowned﴾. It is also read "annahum" with the fatha, meaning: because they are...

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verses 25–26:

﴿How many they left behind﴾ That is: they left behind much (of gardens) in Egypt.

﴿of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾ (meaning) assemblies that were adorned and dwellings that were beautified.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verses 25–26:

﴿How many they left behind﴾ That is: they left behind much (of gardens) in Egypt.

﴿of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾ (meaning) assemblies that were adorned and dwellings that were beautified.

Translation:

﴿And luxury﴾, that is, enjoyment (تَنَعُّم, tana''um).

﴿in which they had been jesting﴾ — living in comfort and enjoying themselves. It is also read as "فَكِهِينَ" (fakihin).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 28:

﴿Thus⦆ The kaf (ك) is in the place of accusative (nasb), and "dhalika" (ذَلِكَ, "that") is a demonstrative referring to a verbal noun (masdar) indicated by "tarakū" (تَرَكُوا, "they left"), i.e.: like that deprivation (salb), We deprived them of it (p-63).

﴿And We caused other people to inherit it﴾ It has also been said: like that expulsion (ikhraj), We expelled them from it. And it has been said: it is in the place of nominative (raf') as a predicate (khabariyya), i.e.: the matter is thus; in that case "awrathnaha" (أوْرَثْناها, "We caused to inherit it") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "tarakū" (تَرَكُوا). And according to the first two views, it is governed by the implied verb (al-fi'l al-muqaddar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 29:

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾ is a metaphor for not caring about their destruction and not regarding their existence as significant. In it there is mockery of them and of their condition, which is contrary to the condition of one whose loss is great, so that it is said of him: "The heaven and the earth wept." From this is what has been related: "Indeed, the believer, over him weep his prayer-place, the place of his worship, the channels through which his deeds ascend, the channels through which his provision descends, and his traces on the earth." It has also been said: its implied meaning is "the people of the heaven and the earth."

﴿And they were not﴾ given respite when the time of their destruction came.

﴿respited﴾ — given a delay until another time, or until the Hereafter; rather, it was hastened for them in this world.

**﴿And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel﴾** by doing to Pharaoh and his people what We did.

**﴿from the humiliating punishment﴾**, namely Pharaoh's enslaving them, slaying their sons, and sparing their women, in a state of subjugation and oppression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 31:

﴿From Pharaoh﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "from the punishment," either by making him the very punishment itself because of his excess in it, or by omitting a genitive-modified noun, meaning: the punishment of Pharaoh. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the humiliating," meaning: being from Pharaoh. It was also read as "man Fir'awn" (﴿مَن فِرْعَوْنُ﴾), in the sense of "Do you know who he is in his arrogance and his acting as Pharaoh?", and the vagueness of his affair at first, followed by its clarification through the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, he was among the exceeding ones, of the transgressors﴾ (second), is a disclosure of the reality of his affair in evil and corruption beyond which nothing more can be added. And the words of the Exalted, ﴿among the transgressors﴾, are either a second predicate of "kāna" (was), meaning: he was arrogant and excessive, or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "ʿāliyan" (exalted), meaning: he was of high rank among the transgressors, surpassing them and extreme in excess.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 32:

﴿And We certainly chose them﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel.

﴿with knowledge﴾, i.e., knowing that they were deserving of being chosen, or knowing that they would deviate at times and that many lapses would come from them.

﴿above the worlds﴾, entirely, due to the great number of prophets among them, or above the worlds of their own time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 33:

﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾ such as the splitting of the sea (falq al-bahr), the shading of the clouds (tazlil al-ghamam), the sending down of manna and quail (al-mann wal-salwa), and other great signs the like of which was not known among others than them.

﴿Wherein was a manifest trial﴾ a clear blessing, or an evident test, to see how they would act (li-nanzura kayfa ya'malun).

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 44, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, these people﴾ meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh, since the discussion concerns them, and the story of Pharaoh and his people is related to indicate their similarity in persisting in misguidance and to warn against the befalling of the like of what befell them ﴿would say﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 35:

﴿There is not but our first death.﴾ That is: the final outcome and the end of the matter is nothing but the first death, which terminates the worldly life, and there is no intention to affirm a second death, as in your saying: "Zayd performed the first pilgrimage (ḥajjah) and died." It has also been said: when it was said to them, "Indeed you will die one death that will be followed by life, just as a death preceded you," they said, "There is not but our first death," meaning: the death that is followed by life is nothing but the first death. It has also been said: the meaning is: death is not except this death, not the death that follows the life of the grave, as you claim.

﴿And we will not be resurrected.﴾ That is, we will not be raised up (mab'ūthūn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 36:

﴿Then bring back our fathers﴾ This is addressed to those who were promised resurrection by the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you claim concerning the establishment of the Hour and the raising of the dead, so that it may become clear that it is true. It has also been said: they used to ask them to pray to God Most High that He raise for them Qusayy ibn Kilab, so that they might consult him, for he was their chief and their refuge in important matters and calamities.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 37:

﴿Are they better?﴾ This is a rejoinder to their claim and a threat to them, meaning: are they better in strength and might, by which the causes of destruction are repelled?

﴿Or the people of Tubba'?﴾ He is Tubba' al-Himyari, who marched with armies, bewildered the (people of) al-Hira (ḥayyara al-ḥīra), and built Samarqand. It was also said that he demolished it, that he was a believer, and that his people were disbelievers; for this reason God, exalted is He, censured them without him. He used to write at the head of his letter: "In the name of God, who possesses a sea and a sea," meaning many seas. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not revile Tubba', for he had embraced Islam." And from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not a prophet." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he was a prophet. It was also said that the kings of Yemen were called al-Tababi'a (Tubba'iyyun) because they were followed (yutba'una), just as they are called al-Aqyal (sing. qayl, a title meaning "ruler") because they hold counsel (yataqayyalun).

﴿And those before them﴾ is a conjunction with "the people of Tubba'," and what is meant by them is 'Ad, Thamud, and their likes, from every obstinate tyrant, "possessors of mighty strength." The interrogative serves to establish that those were stronger than these. His words, exalted is He, ﴿We destroyed them﴾ form a resumptive clause explaining the outcome of their affair. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed they were criminals﴾ give the reason for their destruction, so that it is known that those, when they were destroyed because of their criminality despite being at the utmost of strength and might, then these, who are partners to them in criminality and weaker than them in might and strength, are even more deserving (of destruction).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 38:

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ i.e., what is between the two kinds (jinsayn). It is also read "wa-ma baynahunna" (and what is between them, feminine plural).

﴿in play﴾ (la'ibin), i.e., heedlessly, without there being in their creation any sound purpose or praiseworthy end.

We did not create them
(meaning the heavens and the earth) and what is between them

﴿except with truth﴾. This is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh, "emptied exception") taken from the most general of states or the most general of causes. That is: We did not create them while being connected to any of things, except while being connected to the truth; or, We did not create them through any cause among causes, except through the cause of the truth, which is faith, obedience, resurrection and recompense.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that the matter is so, and therefore they deny resurrection and recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾ i.e., the decision (fasl) of truth from falsehood and the distinguishing of the one who is right from the one who is wrong; or the separation (fasl) of a man from his relatives and loved ones.

﴿is their appointed time﴾ the time of their appointment.

﴿all of them﴾. It is also read "mee-qatahum" (ميقاتَهُمْ) in the accusative, with it being the subject of "inna" (إنَّ, indeed/verily, the particle of emphasis), and "the Day of Decision" (يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ) being its predicate; i.e., indeed the appointed time of their reckoning and their recompense is on the Day of Decision.

(p-65) ﴿Upon the Day when no client (mawla) shall avail another client at all﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Decision," or an attribute (sifa) of "their appointed time," or an adverbial (zarf) of what the Decision indicates, not of itself.

﴿mawla﴾: from kinship or otherwise.

﴿from a mawla﴾: any mawla whatsoever.

﴿shay'an﴾: that is, anything at all of averting.

﴿nor shall they be helped﴾: the pronoun refers to the first "mawla" according to its meaning, because it is general.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 42:

﴿Except for those upon whom Allah has mercy﴾ by pardoning them and accepting intercession on their behalf. Its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal) for the waw (of the plural subject), or in the accusative case as an exception (istithna').

﴿Indeed, He is the Almighty﴾ who cannot be helped by anyone who wishes to punish Him (i.e., whom He wishes to punish).

﴿the Most Merciful﴾ to whomever He wishes to show mercy.

Translation:

﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾. It is also read with the kasra on the shin (إنَّ شِجَرَةَ), and the meaning of zaqqum has already been discussed in Surat al-Saffat.
﴿Ṭaʿām al-Athīm﴾ (the food of the sinner): i.e., the one who commits many sins; and what is meant by it is the disbeliever, as indicated by what precedes it and what follows it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 45:

﴿Like molten brass﴾ (al-muhl), which is that which is heated in the Fire until it melts. It is said: it is the dregs of olive oil (durdi al-zayt).

﴿It boils in the bellies﴾. It is also read with the ta' (tayaghlī, "it boils"), taking the verb as referring back to the tree (al-shajara).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 46:

﴿Like the boiling of scalding water﴾, boiling as its boiling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 47:

﴿Seize him⦄ on the understanding that a speech is implied, and the address is to the angels of punishment (al-zabaniyah).

﴿Drag him⦄ i.e., pull him along. Al-'atl (ʿatl) is seizing a thing by its collar or its middle and dragging it by force and violence. It is also recited with a dammah on the letter tā' (fa-'tulūhu), which is a dialect (lughah) of the same root.

﴿into the midst of the Hellfire⦄ i.e., its midst (wasaṭihi).

Then pour out over his head some of the torment of the boiling water.

The original form would have been: "Boiling water is poured out from above their heads." Then it was said: "Torment is poured out from above their heads, which is the boiling water," for the sake of emphasis (mubalaghah). Then "torment" was made an annexed noun (idafah) to "boiling water" for lightness (takhfif), and "min" was added to indicate (dalalah) that what is poured out is a part of this kind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 49:

﴿Taste it! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ That is: say this to him in mockery and rebuke, for what he used to claim. It is narrated that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Between its two mountains there is no one mightier or nobler than me. By Allah, neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me." And it was recited with a fath (opening vowel) on the hamza of inna, meaning: "Because you..." or "the punishment of [the fact] that you..."

**Verse 44:50:** ﴿Indeed, this﴾ — that is, the punishment.

﴿is what you used to doubt﴾ — you used to be skeptical of it and dispute about it. The plural is used in view of the meaning, since what is intended is the category of the sinner (al-athim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, the God-conscious (al-muttaqun)﴾: that is, those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins.

﴿are in a station﴾: in a place of standing. The intended meaning is "place" in an unrestricted sense, for it is one of the specific terms whose usage has become widespread in the general sense. It is also read with a damma on the mim (maqam), meaning a place of residence.

﴿secure﴾: one in which its occupant is safe from calamities and from being moved away from it. It is from security (amn), which is the opposite of betrayal (khiyana). The place is described with it by way of metaphor, as though a frightening place betrays its occupant because of the hardships encountered in it.

Verse 52: "In gardens and springs" (﴿فِي جَنّاتٍ وعُيُونٍ﴾) is a substitute (badal) for "a place of security" (maqam), brought in to indicate its purity and its containing of the good things of food and drink.

This commentary says that ﴿they will wear garments of fine silk and thick brocade﴾ may be: a second predicate (خَبَرٌ ثانٍ, *khabar thani*), a circumstantial qualifier (حالٌ, *hal*) of the pronoun (ضَمِيرٌ, *damir*) in the prepositional phrase (جارٌّ, *jarr*), or a resumptive new sentence (اسْتِئْنافٌ, *istinaf*).

"Sundus" is the thin silk, and "istabraq" is the thick silk. The word istabraq is arabized (مُعَرَّب, *mu'arrab*), meaning it is a non-Arabic word adopted into Arabic.

﴿reclining face to face﴾: in the assemblies, so that they may find companionship with one another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 54:

﴿Kadhalika﴾ That is: the matter is so, or: thus We bestowed it upon them.

﴿And We shall marry them to houris with large, lovely eyes﴾ according to the attributive reading (ʿalā al-waṣf); it is also read with the construct (iḍāfa), meaning: We joined them with them (qarannāhum bihinna). Al-ḥūr is the plural of al-ḥawrāʾ, which is the one with the white of the eye very white and the iris very black (al-bayḍāʾ). Al-ʿīn is the plural of al-ʿaynāʾ, which is one with large eyes (al-ʿaẓīmat al-ʿaynayn). It has been disputed whether they are women of this world or other than them.

﴿They call for every kind of fruit therein﴾: that is, they ask for and order the bringing of whatever fruits they desire; none of them is restricted to a particular place or time.

﴿Secure﴾: from everything that would harm them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 56:

﴿They shall not taste death therein, except the first death.﴾ Rather, they will continue in life forever. The exception (al-istithna') is either disjunct (munqati') or contiguous (muttasil), on the basis that the purpose is to state the impossibility of tasting death therein at all, as if it were said: "They will not taste death therein, except if it were possible to taste the first death at that time."

﴿And He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim).﴾ It has also been read with the doubled consonant (shaddah), for emphasis in the protection (al-wiqayah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 44, verse 57:

﴿As a bounty from your Lord.﴾ That is: they are given all of that as a gift and favour from Him, exalted is He. It is also recited in the nominative, "fadlun" (فَضْلٌ), meaning: that is a bounty.

﴿That is the supreme triumph.﴾ There is no triumph beyond it, for it is deliverance from all that is hateful and the attainment of every desire.

The words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue, that they may be reminded﴾ (*fadhlakah*, a concluding summary) of the noble surah. That is: We have sent down the Clear Book in your language so that your people may understand it, be reminded, and act in accordance with its requirements, and if they do not do that,

﴿So wait﴾ (for what will befall them).

﴿Indeed, they too are waiting﴾ (for what will befall you). It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ha-Mim (al-Dukhan) on Friday night will be forgiven in the morning."
